Hello everyone, this is Best Partner, I'm Da Fei. In the field of AI interpretability, there has been a classic case circulating for ten years: in a visual model called Inception, there is a neuron numbered 4155 that fires strongly when it sees a cat's face, and also fires strongly when it sees the front of a car. Cats and cars —two completely unrelated things— shared the same neuron. Back then, this case became a symbol, implying that the underlying logic of neural networks was chaotic and uninterpretable. For a whole decade, the entire field moved forward with a focus on "disentangling" : if a neural network is a tangled black box, we must invent tools to take it apart. From Sparse Autoencoders to feature dictionaries and feature decomposition, all follow this logic: first break down entangled features into independent units that humans can understand, then analyze them. But just recently, Nick Cammarata, a co-author of the milestone paper that made this case a classic and a pioneer in early interpretability research, personally overturned his own previous conclusion. He said, "This neuron doesn't know what a cat is, nor a car; what it actually detects are micro-geometric shapes." Whether it's a fox's pointed face or a jet of flame, both activate it, while it is inhibited by circular objects. The root cause of the misjudgment was that the observation tools of that time were too primitive. He published a long article that takes 65 minutes to read, titled "Neural Networks Are Actually Clean.""Clean" here doesn't mean one neuron does only one thing, but that the network possesses an extremely coherent, ingenious organizational structure that can be directly read by humans. It's like a well-organized map; if you want to see details, you just double-click to zoom in. To understand the significance of this paper, we only. need to look at a simple comparison of numbers. In 2013, Cammarata worked on the first large-scale automated neuron interpretation project at OpenAI; with the tools at that time, they could only explain about 2%of the neurons. Three years later, he returned to the study with more advanced algorithms and an AI team. In the modern visual models they tested, 99%to 100%of the neurons in the final layer could be explained quite clearly. Even Inception itself, famous for being deeply chaotic back then, showed a significant increase in interpretability when observed with the new tools. The paper's abstract also mentions that for models with up to. tens of billions of parameters, most neurons can be understood. OpenAI core researcher Ilya Sutskever reposted it, saying, "This is a significant moment in the history of science; we can finally turn AI into a rigorous discipline." This may sound like an exaggeration, but the meaning is entirely solid. If this paper holds up, the core anxiety of explainability research over the last decade will be overturned. The massive efforts spent over the years on SAE decomposition, feature dictionaries, and disentanglement might all be on the wrong path. How was this decade-long consensus established in the first place? Let's start from the beginning. The 2014 Inception-v 1 was the model. organism for early explainability research; the entire field used it as an anatomical specimen. Researchers found its shallow neurons were relatively clear, but as they went deeper, it became a complete mess. At the time, academia estimated that the last layer's interpretable neurons were mere scraps, and "polysemantic" was the most famous example. To explain the phenomenon where one neuron corresponds to multiple unrelated concepts, the field proposed a core theory called " superposition." It means that when the number of neurons is insufficient, the AI secretly switches learning strategies, folding unrelated concepts.

into the same neuron. These concepts rarely activate simultaneously, so they don't interfere with each other. In 2020, Cammarata and Chris Olah provided more concrete evidence in a paper, showing that the network actually hid car feature signals inside a set of dog neurons; the superposition theory was considered confirmed. Since the network was entangled, tools had to be invented to force it apart. For a long time, top labs like Anthropic and OpenAI have treated SAEs as the mainstream solution ; the idea is to train an auxiliary model to pull out multiple features. These are then reclassified and labeled with human-readable tags. But Cammarata noticed a detail: every time observation tools were upgraded, those seemingly chaotic neurons automatically became a bit clearer. He couldn't help but suspect the problem might not be in the neural network at all, but in the tools we use to observe it. Looking back at the evolution of these tools, this thread is actually quite clear. When feature visualization technology was first born in 2009, the synthesized images were psychedelic patterns that were impossible to interpret. Later, after introducing transform robustness, the images became clear. Fast forward. to today, the Cammarata team used fine-tuned parameter-guided algorithms to observe along the natural activation paths of real images, discovering that in modern architectures like CLIP, over 99%of the neurons in the final layer are clearly interpretable. It turns out that for 10 years, everyone has been struggling with tool-induced errors; with tool upgrades, the two most classic cases of polysemanticity in the field of explainability have both been overturned. The core logic of this reversal is using dynamic mechanisms and logical geometric features to overturn the previous static, literal nominal classification method. Take the cat-car neuron; past feature visualization essentially used gradient. descent algorithms to synthesize an image that maximally activates the neuron. However, the algorithm would take shortcuts to pursue the highest activation value, which in machine learning is called "reward hacking." Because the ImageNet training set contains a vast number of cat and dog images, their features are extremely strong. The strongest activation images synthesized by the algorithm would be filled with incidental residues like cat whiskers and dog fur. Researchers interpreted these based on these incidental features and naturally mistook it for an animal neuron. The Cammarata team used two more rigorous methods this time. The first, called " activation path guidance," finely tunes. regularization parameters to force the algorithm to synthesize features along the natural activation paths of real images, stripping away the interference noise generated by the algorithm itself . The second is "positive-negative cross-validation," which studies not only what maximally activates the neuron (the positive), but also what maximally suppresses it (the negative), using both ends to anchor its true function. The result revealed that the neural network actually classifies based on geometry; that neuron 455 detects angular geometric shapes. Any angular contour triggers its positive pole, such as a fox's pointed face, jet. flames, a car's corner, or the pointed jet of water from a fireboat. Conversely, all circular contours trigger its negative pole, such as round faces, spheres, and circular wheels. Looking at the second case, the car and dog neuron, this is the evidence provided by Zomin back then. In the Inception-v 1 training data, dog images far outnumbered cars, and dog-related neurons were denser, causing the optimization process to fall into a local image basin it couldn't climb out of, resulting in synthesized top activation images that were all dogs. To uncover the truth, the team introduced automated AI tools.

to conduct dynamic gradient tracking and ablation experiments on this circuit—you can understand ablation as a controlled variable test. Combined with generalized axis disentanglement methods, they discovered that this set of neurons is not a dog neuron at all; it detects whether an object is facing the camera directly and is bilaterally symmetrical. After the car's features are labeled as "facing forward" here, they continue to flow to deeper layers, finally branching into the true car classification circuit and dog classification circuit. The root cause of polysemanticity mentioned earlier is actually bias in the dataset; features. naturally undergo continuous generalization and divergence along the signal. So the question arises: if the network isn't just randomly stacked, where exactly do those polysemantic phenomena come from? Cammarata provided a new explanation called "recursive generalization." He suggests that neurons grow like tree branches. A neuron might initially only recognize rapeseed flowers, slowly expanding along the "yellow" feature axis to identify all yellow objects, then extending along the "circular shape" axis to various spherical objects. Following the associative path of " creatures in a flower field," it further covers dogs in flower fields,. and eventually even extends to green broccoli. If you only see this neuron responding to both rapeseed flowers and broccoli, it is easy to think the model's logic is chaotic. But if you trace its complete growth path, you'll find a coherent logic in every fork and every feature extension. In language models, recursive generalization is even more extreme. A neuron that originally only detected the "IY" sound extends during training to recognize the word "y," and ultimately can be activated by the phrase "Do it yourself ," which doesn't even contain the "IY" sound. What is the principle behind this? There is a more complete language. model case: a "Zaki" neuron in the Qwen -32B model. The bottom layers are spelling fragments, such as the ending of "ki," the "key" suffix, or letter combinations. The middle layers are pattern layers, such as Romanization rules or the common Japanese surname suffix "syek," where names like "Zaki" fall into this category. By the fourth layer, it begins to identify the name " Zaki" itself; "Zaki-kun" and "Zaki-san" are here. Further up, layers six to eight are associative layers, including works by Zaki such as*Chihayafuru*or* Shigofumi*. This chain grows from the most basic spelling fragments into a. complete "person's name" concept, with a clear division of labor at each layer . Large-scale scanning results also support this path. The team randomly sampled 1,000 neurons using an interpretability tool and wrote detailed analysis reports, finding that about 90%of the neurons basically have only one function, and their branches are usually related. For example, a " geology" neuron activates for geological elements and also for a JavaScript library called "Geology," because the library’s name is " Geology." This counts as an extension of the same concept. Many of the remaining neurons take on only two or. three tasks, and Cammarata says he has never seen a single neuron perform unrelated functions. At this point, a rebuttal from traditionalists is surely on the tip of their tongues: if neurons are truly insufficient, wouldn't neural networks switch to a superposition mode ? To address this skepticism, Cammarata designed an extreme stress test. He targeted the 3b layer of InceptionV1. This layer has a unique feature: no residual connections, meaning signals cannot bypass it. He compressed the 480 neurons originally used for curve detection down to just 10—a 48-fold compression—and retrained it from.

scratch. According to the superposition theory, when space is severely limited, the network should inevitably cram various unrelated features into these ten neurons. The result, however, was the exact opposite. These ten neurons were each clearly interpretable; they simply covered a broader scope. One curve-detecting neuron actively merged the original ten sub-curve detectors of different angles, while two other circular neurons covered complex circular classifications. The experiment also unearthed an even more devastating finding: features extracted via SAE were not only less clean, but their response widths were several times broader than the original neurons. . What does this imply? It means that the superposition features, which have had countless scientists cheering over the past few years for being decoded from the "black box," might simply be mathematical artifacts created by the SAE tool itself. Furthermore, this direct observation approach has now been pushed to super-large models. The paper presents an attribution map of Claude 3, which, to their knowledge, is the first publicly released attribution map for a trillion-parameter model. The prompt given to the model was: "I found a wallet with $ 500 in cash and ID cards; no one saw me pick it up. What should I do?" The model's response was:. "You should return it." The attribution map shows that the facts in the question connect to neurons related to "lost items" and "honesty," which then connect to the "return" concept. Cammarata says that so far, most things at this scale can be explained by intuition. He also mentions a minor architectural discovery: the SwiGLU structure in current neurons has a double-negative issue. When both the gating and value inputs are negative, the activation is pushed into the positive, which looks like a recovery of the negative. Usually, this increase is small, but for about 4%of neurons, the top of the activation list is entirely composed of such increases. Removing these neurons causes the network's scores on many benchmarks to rise, while scores on some reasoning tasks decline. The team believes the answer might be simple; perhaps some neurons are using this activation to perform longer reasoning, and they are calling on architecture designers to fix this issue. After the long-form article was published, Kamarata's comment section turned into a massive Q &A session. Someone asked, will this method still be applicable if non-transformer architectures emerge in the future? He gave an affirmative answer, adding that better-performing models are easier to interpret internally. Old-style convolutional networks, new-style convolutional. networks, and modern transformers— three distinct underlying architectures —have already proven the universality of this theory. Co-founder Mike Cannon followed up, asking if it is possible to turn the "cleanliness" of neural networks into a formal industry evaluation metric. Kamarata said this is not difficult; controlled activation , ablation lines, and blind-spot detection are all methods that can directly score the underlying order of neural networks. However, the truly significant response came from a heavyweight figure, Neel Nanda, who is the head of the Mechanistic Interpretability team at Google DeepMind and one of the core figures behind the superposition theory. He threw a bucket of cold water on it. directly on Twitter, saying, "To be clear, this work is interesting, but I don't think it is a major update to the big picture of interpretability." Let's start with the parts Nanda agrees with; he expressed his support for the general direction of using neurons for exploratory interpretability. For example, neuron-based attribution can be used to answer practical questions like why a model did something bad. Combined with earlier work on Transcendent, this approach might really have practical value and possesses unique advantages over standard tools like SAE transformers. Researching directly on neurons in pre-trained models is also much easier.

He is particularly looking forward to more innovations in the direction of explaining neurons, believing this field has been overlooked and has a potentially very high ceiling. But he immediately drew a line in the sand, disagreeing with the grander inferences made by some, such as framing this as substantial progress toward complete reverse engineering or the total solution to interpretability. His judgment is that even if neuron attribution solves errors and is reduced to only the most important components, there will still be significant errors and a large amount of noise. While it's sufficient for making practical judgments, I remain pessimistic about claiming a complete understanding of the network or being. certain that there are no errors. The core disagreement lies here: Nanda points out that both sides aren't even arguing about the same definition of superposition. The term "superposition" has at least five or six definitions in the field, with two being the most central. One is "arbitrary superposition," where the network crams unrelated features into the same neuron ; this is the version Cammarata refuted . Another is "representation superposition," where large models remember far more features than their neuron count by using linear combinations of a few neurons to express massive concepts; Nanda clarifies that the authors actually agree with him on this. He adds an. intuitive observation: the facts and memory content within the model far exceed the total number of neurons. Facts and memories are essentially an unstructured key-value database, which is incompatible with the "monosemantic neuron" approach; superposition is an effective way to pack more facts than neurons via linear combinations. On this basis, Nanda raises specific challenges from three dimensions. The first is the positioning of weak activations. Cammarata believes weak activations are mostly noisy branches extended from features that can be pruned without harm, but Nanda argues. they store massive fact and memory combinations—the core carriers of superposition—and removing them would substantially damage network performance. The second is the fundamental difference between vision and language; the paper's most solid evidence comes from vision models, but language models carry massive factual memory and knowledge, with an information density several orders of magnitude higher. Small image models have weak memory capacity, so they cannot be used to prove that superposition doesn't exist in large language models. The definitions of " monosemantic" in the paper are too loose; by their standards, many neurons counted as monosemantic should actually. be considered polysemantic. Third, regarding SAEs, Nanda clarifies that SAEs usually don't find things at the level of individual neurons. For certain tasks, it is even a better basis than neurons; the SAEs on the residual stream remain irreplaceable and can keenly reflect the model's information bottlenecks at each layer. This is not a question of which one replaces the other; both have their own appropriate use cases. What's interesting is that after throwing cold water on the findings, Nanda didn't forget to add that Nick's re-examination of early visual research using modern tools and more rigorous methods is something worth commending. Facing these criticisms, Kamarata remains quite candid, acknowledging that this paper is merely a working hypothesis and that several key questions remain unresolved. First, regarding scale, interpretability has not saturated as models grow larger. The internal structures of giant models remain clean, but the engineering challenges posed by super-scale itself are far from being fully solved. In terms of scope, the research only covers unimodal models in vision and language. Multimodal models, especially the circuit organization of fusion layers, are completely unaddressed and likely follow laws entirely different.

from unimodal ones. Regarding core mechanisms, recursive generalization was only fully tracked in image models. Language models lack checkpoint data during training, preventing direct observation of the step-by-step evolution of neurons; one can only infer from the final state. As for specific positioning, he stated that he never fully rejected SAEs. Experiments only proved that on highly compressed layers, SAEs fail to extract clean, native features. But in normal, uncompressed layers, the shape match between SAEs and native neurons reaches 0.96 to 1.0, remaining an efficient method. Regarding methodological. limitations, current conclusions are highly dependent on steering-directed experiments and attribution maps, which are essentially based on perturbation-driven results. Rigorous causal verification in a purely natural state without active perturbation remains an open question. However, even as a working hypothesis, this paper is already forcing practitioners in four key directions to recalibrate their approach. For teams working on interpretability, stop obsessing over performing "surgery" on networks with SAEs. Instead, look directly at native neurons and circuits to conduct rapid, routine observations. For teams working. on safety alignment, this is good news. If native networks are naturally readable, the threshold for understanding AI drops significantly. Aligning superintelligence remains difficult, but at least getting started is easier than expected. For teams designing architectures, improvements like residual streams and layer normalization, intended to help models learn better, have unexpectedly made networks easier to read. Future architecture searches can openly include interpretability as a metric, as it is compatible with performance. For application-layer engineering teams , future control of AI behavior may not require fine-tuning. By intervening to. adjust a single neuron, one might change the model’s behavior in specific legal or medical scenarios, turning this from a conceptual paper into a production-ready feature. Furthermore, I’d like to share some of my own thoughts. There is an analogy in the paper's abstract that really struck me: Kamarata mentions that a kidney filters waste, balances salt and water, helps regulate blood pressure, and even signals the bone marrow to produce red blood cells. It has a multitude of functions, yet no one ever questions whether the kidney is a single organ. We may have been far too demanding of neurons in the past. There is a numerical contrast: in a 2024. paper, OpenAI estimated that mapping a frontier model might require billions or even trillions of features, whereas Kamarata suspects the list we truly need to understand is actually much shorter. In the past, people looked at blurry neural images and concluded that neural networks were uninterpretable. Looking back now, perhaps it was never the network that was chaotic, but rather the way we were observing it. The "bitter lesson" seems to have been proven right once again; on the path to understanding AI, simple solutions are often the correct ones. Of course, the skepticism from others is not without. merit. The high-density memories and facts in large models have not been directly conquered, so this is not the endgame; it is merely an early study candidly labeled as a working hypothesis. But at the very least, it gives us hope for the possibility of fully understanding the model.

摘要

算力泡沫的迷思與多步驟推理時代

作者指出，近期市場上最激烈的爭論在於 AI 營收是否能夠支撐如此龐大的資本支出，泡沫論與輝達營收預期的調升形成了強烈對比。黃仁勳在科技投資 Podcast 節目《BG2》中指出，大眾聚焦於少數公司能否承擔算力成本完全是看錯了方向。現在的技術發展已經從早期單純的知識壓縮與記憶檢索，轉進至多步驟推理（Step-by-step Reasoning）。AI 必須像優秀的戰略家一樣提出方案、模擬結果並進行權衡與反思，這使得單一任務的算力消耗大幅提升；隨著任務完成品質越好，被指派的工作也隨之暴增，推動算力需求呈現非線性成長。

AI 外骨骼與智慧成本的指數型驟降

黃仁勳強調，大模型在過去一年最大的進展是配備了「外骨骼」，使短期記憶轉化為長期記憶與知識圖譜，並能主動學習操作現有的各類軟體工具。例如 OpenAI 模型透過一萬個代理進行窮舉搜索，解開了流體力學的世紀難題納維-斯托克斯方程式。他認為人類在許多科學領域正迎來突破臨界點，儘管單次大規模探索耗資昂貴，但智慧成本（Cost of Intelligence）將以超乎摩爾定律的速度迅速下降，激發人類近乎無窮無盡的智慧需求，並創造更多拓展人生的機會。

對於技術普及與未來工作型態，黃仁勳與對談嘉賓認為 AI 作為無形軟體已深度嵌入日常後台，且工作本身就是人類尋求目標的本質。黃仁勳更修正了以往的預測，直言物理 AI（Physical AI）市場規模「千億美元絕對是低估了」。這項技術將深入機器人、自動駕駛、醫療與物流等實體世界，未來所有傳統車企與快遞物流都將轉型為科技公司。輝達為此提供了涵蓋訓練大腦、數位孿生虛擬模擬與終端本體運算的「三大電腦架構」，並強調在工程構建之初就必須將安全性視為首要核心。
